en: My father and that valiant man
Were sons of two brothers.
Light on a horse, fit even for a colt,
Sleepless, watchful on the road,
His waist firmly girded,
If seven tumens of enemies came,
He would charge in with his coat flung open.
His waist girded superbly,
If six great hosts of Chinese foes appeared,
He would plunge among them and attack.
A sharp edge of black steel,
Syrgak of my leopard khan father,
In the fighting against the Khagan,
In the battle with mighty Beijing,
When he reached twenty-one,
He fell to a bullet.
“Younger brother, ride this way!” he said.
On the narrow path within the water
He escorted him.
On the near side of him,
Who had gone before the caliph and received a writ,
Known among mortals as Bakai the Leopard,
Whose blessing enriched the people,
Whose watchfulness brought people light,
Wearing a gray lynx-fur cap,
Wielding a mottled-blue shield,
Who found words in a sudden crisis,
Who found sight in the dark of night,
My father Sultan Manas
He had led with him and made a warrior,
Made him equal to a hero's son.
Leading my father with him,
He swept away those he set his gaze upon.
The enemies who opposed him
He leveled with the black earth.
He planted him and made a garden.
My generous father Manas
He built up into a dwelling.
The very son of saintly wisdom,
Allah's own beloved servant,
Noble Bakai, the sheltering hero,
Bakai the Leopard, the noble lion,
When he reached eleven years of age,
Those who beheld his majesty were afraid.
He studied five years in Mecca.
Receiving blessings from learned men,
He became known as Bakai the Lion.
The two cities, Egypt and Jerusalem—
He studied five years there.
In those cities, pillars of the faith,
My uncle Bakai the Lion
Had attained profound learning.
Ruin-bringing Bakai, khan and sultan,
On a horse like a gray tulpar,
“My son, cross without fear,
Attain your heart's desire,” he said.
“We knew long ago that you would come.
My child, we have worried over your crossing.
Not merely from flowing water, my foal,
Do not draw back even from death.
When you charge the enemy in battle,
Raise ‘Manas!’ as your battle cry.
My child, do not turn back from death!”
My uncle Bakai, the lion-hearted hero,
Appearing just as he always had,
Urged him onward.
When he looked behind him,
Mounted on a horse like Kartkurong,
Wearing a chosen bulletproof coat,
Going about without wrongdoing,
He knew seventy different languages.
Rival to all mankind,
Of fortunate Manas, the warrior lion,
The interpreter in this world,
When sent into black embers,
He knew the Kalmyk language.
When sent into red-hot shot,
He knew the Chinese language.
The two tribes, Solon and Shibe—
He knew their languages.
The Russians on his right—
He knew their language.
The Frankish people before him—
He knew their different speech.
Ah, a leopard when roused to anger,
To my father whom Kydyr had blessed,
My precious Azhibai had been granted thus.
From beside him Azhibai said:
“Orphan child, cross without fear!
If you survive, my foal,
May you attain your desire!”
Making Kartkurong lunge,
Surging like a woman whose husband had died,
My warrior father's Azhibai
Drove him onward once again.
Who knows—we cannot say if it is true—
Appearing as they were in life,
The heroes came to his aid.
Behind him was a marvel:
My leopard father, the bloodthirsty lion,
His orphan who looked to him for support—
That was where he came to help him.
Long ago my father, Khan Manas,
When all the peoples rose,
And formed forty-two vast hosts,
With all the Muslim people there,
With giants Koshoi and Toshtuk among them,
With skilled spearmen there,
Who never shrank from death,
With mighty men of surpassing courage,
With all the saints there,
With the peoples of twelve khans,
My father the khan stood in their midst.
“I shall scatter the infidels' wealth,
I shall open the Muslims' road.
Into great, looming Beijing
I shall enter straight and thrust my spear.
The Prophet is true, your faith is true;
From the looming hell
I shall free my soul.
Against haughty Beijing
I shall charge and thrust my spear.
Against Beijing beyond the reach of the Flood
I shall wage an unrelenting holy war.
Against Beijing where the Prophet never trod
I shall advance in holy war.
Against highly honored Beijing
I shall gather the Muslim host.
Those infidels seething there
I shall bring to the Muslim faith.
If they do not prize my words,
If they do not enter the faith I urge,
The Khagan's many people
I shall drive before me and slaughter.
I shall strip Beijing's people bare.
With the Khagan's khan at their head,
I shall call them to the Muslim faith.”
He went and attacked Beijing,
Taking much booty of gold.
Against Beijing that Solomon could not take,
Over the tormented city of Beijing
My father ruled as khan for six months.
He lost his mighty warriors,
And after six months all was over.
From Beijing with its Khagan,
My warrior father whose death had come,
Riding the steed Akkula,
Wearing a white ribbed-cloth coat,
His face like wheat gleaming with oil,
His eyes like twilight mist,
When he turned to face you,
He had the aspect of a dragon.
If you looked from behind,
He had the majesty of six thousand warriors.
There in the water, ah, the orphan's
Heart was sorely troubled.
His father, the fierce-maned Lion,
Appeared as though alive,
Thundering in his wrath.
My leopard father came pounding on,
The youngest of six lions,
The servant beloved of Allah.
From behind, my dear father supported me:
That was when he drove me onward.
“When you enter a battle of gunfire,
Roar in your wrath.
When you face an enemy in dire straits,
My son, raise Manas as your battle cry.
If my spirit is present,
My son, I shall help you everywhere.
My son, I shall always watch over you!”
Seeing him come to his aid,
The boy's heart was stirred.
The spirits of the lion warriors
Appeared just as they had in life.
Coming out of the water, the orphan child
Implored the one God,
Vowing a horse to the one God,
To his father's spirit
He promptly vowed a white-gray mare.
He crossed ridge after ridge,
Traversing many sloping upland meadows.
The orphan Semetey grew excited.
Ken-Shor, where his father had passed away—
Your orphan reached that place.
“My dear mother had told me:
‘At Ken-Shor, where your father died,
There is a great marker,’ she said.”
Long ago, when my father went to Beijing,
When he slaughtered the Khagan's men,
When from the Black Chinese and Manchu
He seized their khanate,
Of the little band of the Islamic faith,
Those who had survived
Had then taken their fill of booty.
Ah, Zhang-zhung's daughter Birmyskal,
And Esenkan's daughter Burulcha—
When he took those two girls as tribute,
The Khagan's khan rallied his strength.
When he unleashed a fierce slaughter,
The spearheads clashed,
And my father fought in earnest.
Muzburchak and Khan Kokcho died.
All who encountered Beijing died.
Those blessed by Kydyr died.
The peoples who encountered Beijing died together.
Those who came died; the khan died.
All who met the Khagan died.
Kokotoy's sole warrior son,
Bokmurun, went there and died.
Serek and Syrgak the Wolf died.
Akayar and Baichoro,
Both those giants died.
Long ago, when Akkula fell to a bullet,
My father had seen Almambet die a martyr.
My father returned from striking the Khagan,
Bereft of Khan Chubak.
“I shall destroy the Khagan,” he had said,
And had his saddle straps gathered up.
While saying his prayers in Beijing,
Through his back, ah,
My father had his lung pierced by a thrust.
Returning ill from Beijing,
My formidable father, that noble lion,
Perished from this world.
That was where he went to the next world,
Smoothing his fine mustache.
That was where he went to Judgment Day,
The place my leopard father died,
The place my dear mother suffered.
Lingering at his bedside,
My poor mother, whom I cherish,
Lost my khan father
When she was thirty-two years old.
On the hills were horses with white-marked heads,
Argymaks and fine steeds mingled.
To cry out and serve him,
I who remained behind was too young.
The place my bloodthirsty father died,
The place my mother watched over him.
Smoothing his fine mustache,
His soul drawing toward Judgment Day,
Coughing in sharp bursts,
Lifting his head from the pillow,
When he tried to rise, groaning,
Blood came gushing out.
Her wailing split the rocks;
My mother's strength failed.
Coughing with heavy thuds,
Lifting his head from the bed,
When he tried to rise, groaning,
Blood poured out by the shovelful.
Born to grief, she cried aloud.
My poor, enslaved mother's strength failed.
With the blood from my father's mouth
Twelve pits were filled.
